chapters.title: Ch 1 · Introduction, value delivery and the 12 principles
Ch 2 · Organizational context: strategy, structure, culture
Ch 4 · Development approach, agile, Scrum and DevOps

questions.q: Every employee must switch to a new company-wide calendar on the same day, and there is no practical way to run the old and new calendars side by side. Which migration strategy is this?
questions.e: A flash cut switches everyone at once. It is fast but needs careful planning, testing and a back-out plan.

questions.q: A team changes its software for new requirements, but the system's fundamental structure stays the same. What is this?
questions.e: Maintenance changes the software while keeping its structure. Architectural transformation changes the structure.

questions.q: A legacy mainframe system moves to a client-server architecture, driven by cheaper server hardware and by users expecting a graphical interface. What is driving this change?
o: Cheaper hardware and demand for a GUI
A need for distributed access alone
A need for stronger data security
questions.e: Hardware cost and user-interface expectations are two of the drivers for architectural transformation.

questions.q: Updating an application so it runs on a new operating system version is which type of maintenance?
questions.e: Adaptive maintenance adapts software to a new environment. Corrective fixes faults; perfective adds new requirements.

questions.q: “As a system changes, its structure degrades unless work is done to keep it simple.” Which of Lehman's laws is this?
questions.e: Increasing complexity: change makes the structure worse unless effort goes into simplifying it.

questions.q: The team notices that defects are rising and each change takes longer than the last. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The team needs a new CCB
questions.e: Rising defects and longer change times are process signs that the system is getting harder to maintain.

questions.q: In agile change control, a change control board approves every product change.
questions.e: Agile has no CCB: the customer owns product changes and the team owns process changes.

questions.q: Parallel operation runs the old and new systems at the same time for a period.
questions.e: It is safe but expensive, because both systems must be run and compared.

questions.q: Maintenance usually costs less than the original development.
questions.e: Maintenance can cost 2 to 100 times as much as development over a system's life.

questions.q: A back-out plan says how to return to the old system if the migration fails.
questions.e: Every migration, especially a flash cut, needs one.

questions.q: Match each maintenance type to an example.
pairs: Fixing a crash that users reported
Moving the app to a new database server
Adding an export feature users asked for

questions.q: Match each migration strategy to its description.
pairs: Everyone switches to the new system at once
Old and new systems run side by side for a while
Rolled out one location or module at a time
Tried first with one small group of users

questions.qc: Put the integrated change control steps in order.
questions.q: Put the integrated change control steps in order. Match each step to its position.
pairs: Recognize the need for a change

questions.qc: Which of these is a product-focused recovery step?
questions.q:
Scenario: Drowning project
A project is six weeks behind schedule. The customer keeps adding requirements, one module causes most of the defects, and the team has no clear view of how far along it really is.

Which of these is a product-focused recovery step?
o: Add miniature milestones to track work
Replace the project manager at once
Have the team work every weekend
questions.e: Product steps stabilize requirements, raise the bar on change requests and trim the feature set.

questions.qc: Adding several new developers now is a safe way to win back the lost six weeks.
questions.q:
Scenario: Drowning project
A project is six weeks behind schedule. The customer keeps adding requirements, one module causes most of the defects, and the team has no clear view of how far along it really is.

Adding several new developers now is a safe way to win back the lost six weeks.
questions.e: Brooks's law: adding people to a late project makes it later.

questions.qc: Name the three core options for a project in trouble.
questions.q:
Scenario: Drowning project
A project is six weeks behind schedule. The customer keeps adding requirements, one module causes most of the defects, and the team has no clear view of how far along it really is.

Name the three core options for a project in trouble.
questions.m: Cut the size of the software, increase process productivity, or slip the schedule (with damage control).
k: Cut the size of the software

questions.q: In an agile project, who owns product changes and who owns process changes?
questions.m: The customer, usually through the product owner, owns product changes. The team owns process changes. (There is no change control board; the PM just facilitates.)
k: The customer (product owner) owns product changes

questions.q: Name three of Lehman's laws.
questions.m: Any three of: continuing change, increasing complexity, large program evolution, organizational stability, conservation of familiarity.

questions.q: A government payroll system has legally fixed, fully documented requirements and uses a technology stack the vendor has delivered many times. Which development approach fits best?
questions.e: Stable requirements and proven technology are exactly when waterfall works well.

questions.q: A startup builds a feature on a brand-new AI API, has six weeks to show investors something, and is still deciding what the feature should do. Which approach fits best?
o: Sequential (waterfall) SDLC with big up-front planning
Ad hoc code-and-fix with no formal process or planning
DevOps focused purely on CI/CD pipeline automation
questions.e: Unclear requirements and new technology call for an evolutionary approach that plans in waves.

questions.q: A team wants a framework for planning and running sprints, but not one that dictates how they test and code. What should they adopt?
questions.e: Scrum is a management framework; it leaves engineering practices to the team. XP prescribes them.

questions.q: Deployments keep breaking because developers hand code over to operations and each side blames the other. What addresses this?
questions.e: DevOps builds a shared culture and pipeline between development and operations.

questions.q: A backlog item has been refined, estimated and is clear enough to pull into a sprint. Which state is it in?
questions.e: Items move from ready for consideration, to ready for refinement, to ready for implementation.

questions.q: In the iterative (unified) process, which phase is considered the most critical?
questions.e: Elaboration settles the architecture and the main risks, so everything after depends on it.

questions.q: In an agile project, which side of the triple constraint is estimated rather than fixed?
questions.e: Agile fixes time and cost and lets scope flex. Waterfall fixes scope and estimates time and cost.

questions.q: Two developers share one computer: one writes code while the other reviews each line. Which XP practice is this?
questions.e: Pair programming puts two people on one piece of code for continuous review.

questions.q: In Scrum, the ScrumMaster owns and orders the product backlog.
questions.e: The product owner owns the backlog. The ScrumMaster coaches the team and removes impediments.

questions.q: Late integration and late risk resolution are symptoms of a waterfall project in trouble.
questions.e: Problems surface only at the end, when they are most expensive to fix.

questions.q: Valuing working software over comprehensive documentation means agile teams do not write documentation.
questions.e: The value is a preference, not a ban: documentation still matters, working software matters more.

questions.q: Deployment frequency and mean time to recover are DevOps metrics.
questions.e: The four are deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and mean time to recover.

questions.q: Complete each Agile Manifesto value.
Match each Scrum term to its meaning.
pairs: A 2–4 week time-box that produces an increment
Decides what is built and in what order
Coaches the team and removes impediments
A short daily sync on progress and blockers

questions.qc: Put the phases of the iterative (unified) process in order.
questions.q: Put the phases of the iterative (unified) process in order. Match each step to its position.

questions.qc: Which approach fits the project overall?
questions.q:
Scenario: FinPay wallet
A bank's team is building a mobile wallet. Regulators require a documented security design before launch. Marketing wants new features every two weeks. The operations team complains that releases often break production.

Which approach fits the project overall?
questions.e: The regulated security design needs up-front, documented work, while features can be delivered in short iterations.

questions.qc: Adopting DevOps practices would help with the broken releases.
questions.q:
Scenario: FinPay wallet
A bank's team is building a mobile wallet. Regulators require a documented security design before launch. Marketing wants new features every two weeks. The operations team complains that releases often break production.

Adopting DevOps practices would help with the broken releases.
questions.e: Shared ownership, automated pipelines and monitoring target exactly that problem.

questions.qc: Name two DevOps metrics the team should track.
questions.q:
Scenario: FinPay wallet
A bank's team is building a mobile wallet. Regulators require a documented security design before launch. Marketing wants new features every two weeks. The operations team complains that releases often break production.

Name two DevOps metrics the team should track.
questions.m: Any two of: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, mean time to recover (MTTR).

questions.q: How does the triple constraint differ between waterfall and agile?
questions.m: Waterfall fixes the scope and estimates time and cost. Agile fixes time and cost and estimates (flexes) the scope.
k: Waterfall fixes scope; time and cost are estimated
Agile fixes time and cost; scope is estimated

questions.q: What does the product owner focus on, and what does the ScrumMaster focus on?
questions.m: The product owner is product-focused: what to build and in what order (the backlog). The ScrumMaster is team-focused: coaching the team, guarding the process and removing impediments.
k: Product owner: the product (what to build, backlog, value)
ScrumMaster: the team and process (impediments, coaching)

questions.q: A vendor bids well below the realistic cost of a government contract, planning to recover the loss later through change orders. Which estimation approach and which risk is this?
o: Priced to win, with the "priced to lose" risk
Wideband Delphi, with a failure to reach consensus
Analogy, with a poorly matched past project
questions.e: Priced to win sets the estimate by what wins the bid; underbidding on purpose is its “priced to lose” risk.

questions.q: Early in a project, with good data from similar past projects, which method fits best?
questions.e: Analogy uses actual historical data and works before a WBS exists. Bottom-up needs a WBS.

questions.q: Experts estimate alone and anonymously, discuss the differences, then estimate again until they agree. Which method is this?
questions.e: Wideband Delphi repeats anonymous estimates and group discussion until consensus.

questions.q: What does the cone of uncertainty show?
o: Estimates grow more accurate as the project goes on
Estimates grow less accurate as the project goes on
Risk exposure peaks in the final project phase
Effort and duration always change together
questions.e: Early estimates can be off by 0.25× to 4×; they converge toward 1× as the team learns more.

questions.q: A 400 KLOC real-time avionics system with tight hardware constraints is which COCOMO mode?
questions.e: Embedded: over 300 KLOC, complex, tight constraints. Intermediate is a model level, not a mode.

questions.q: “Work expands to fill the time available” is a danger of which estimation error?
questions.e: That is Parkinson's law, a risk of estimates that are too generous.

questions.q: Duration equals effort divided by the number of people working on it.
questions.e: For example 60 person-days with 3 people is 20 working days.

questions.q: Bottom-up estimation is quick and works well before a WBS exists.
questions.e: Bottom-up is accurate but slow, and it needs a WBS.

questions.q: Function points measure size by what the software does for its users, not by its lines of code.
questions.e: They count inputs, outputs, inquiries, files and interfaces.

questions.q: In basic COCOMO, development time is calculated directly from KLOC.
questions.e: TDEV = c × E^d uses the effort E, which comes from KLOC.

questions.q: Match each estimation method to its description.
pairs: A quick estimate for the whole project from its overall traits
The sum of estimates for every task in the WBS
Based on actual data from a similar past project
Set by what the customer will pay or the bid needs
Experienced people estimate from their own knowledge

questions.q: Three-point estimate: optimistic 4 days, most likely 7 days, pessimistic 16 days. What is the expected duration?
An organic project is 20 KLOC (a = 2.4, b = 1.05). What is the effort E?

questions.qc: Effort E
questions.q:
Scenario: TechNova (Final 242 style)
TechNova is building an organic system estimated at 32 KLOC. Basic COCOMO constants for organic mode: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38.

Effort E

questions.qc: Development time TDEV
questions.q:
Scenario: TechNova (Final 242 style)
TechNova is building an organic system estimated at 32 KLOC. Basic COCOMO constants for organic mode: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38.

Development time TDEV

questions.qc: Average staff size
questions.q:
Scenario: TechNova (Final 242 style)
TechNova is building an organic system estimated at 32 KLOC. Basic COCOMO constants for organic mode: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38.

Average staff size
questions.e: Staff = E ÷ TDEV = 91.3 ÷ 13.9 ≈ 6.6 people.

questions.qc: Productivity
questions.q:
Scenario: TechNova (Final 242 style)
TechNova is building an organic system estimated at 32 KLOC. Basic COCOMO constants for organic mode: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38.

Productivity
questions.e: Productivity = LOC ÷ E = 32,000 ÷ 91.3 ≈ 350 LOC per staff-month.

questions.qc: Name two other estimation techniques you could use to cross-check this COCOMO result.
questions.q:
Scenario: TechNova (Final 242 style)
TechNova is building an organic system estimated at 32 KLOC. Basic COCOMO constants for organic mode: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38.

Name two other estimation techniques you could use to cross-check this COCOMO result.
questions.m: Any two, for example analogy with past TechNova projects and a bottom-up estimate from the WBS.

questions.q: What is the difference between effort and duration?
questions.m: Effort is the total amount of work, measured in person-time (person-days or staff-months). Duration is the elapsed working time it takes; duration = effort ÷ people.
k: Duration: elapsed calendar or working time

questions.q: Give one advantage and one limitation of COCOMO.
questions.m: Advantage: it is repeatable and based on historical data, so different people get the same answer. Limitation: it needs a size estimate in lines of code, which is hard to know early, and it ignores factors such as requirement volatility.

questions.q: A bank decides which of its projects, programs and ongoing operations to fund this year, choosing the ones that best serve its strategy. What is this top-level grouping called?
questions.e: A portfolio groups projects, programs and operations and manages them together to meet strategic objectives. A program is narrower: related projects managed together for shared benefits.

questions.q: Before choosing a database, an architect studies how the choice will affect the payment service, the support team and future reporting. Which principle is she applying?
questions.e: Systems thinking means recognizing, evaluating and responding to how the parts of a system interact.

questions.q: A PM sets aside money for the risks the team has already identified, and controls that money directly. What is it called?
questions.e: Contingency reserve covers identified risks (known unknowns) and sits inside the cost baseline under the PM's control. Management reserve covers unknown events and is added on top of the baseline.

questions.q: The team prefers to finish the UI design before starting front-end coding because that is their best practice, although the two could overlap. Which dependency is this?
questions.e: A discretionary dependency is a choice based on best practice. A mandatory one comes from a contract or the nature of the work.

questions.q: Two experienced engineers read the requirement “fast checkout” and understand it in two different ways. Which aspect of uncertainty is this?
questions.e: Conceptual ambiguity is a lack of shared understanding, such as people using the same words to mean different things. Situational ambiguity is when more than one outcome is possible.

questions.q: Which of these is a leading indicator?
o: The rate of new change requests
questions.e: Leading indicators predict what will happen; the others are only known after the fact (lagging).

questions.q: A company adapts its standard delivery approach to its own governance policies and culture, before looking at any single project. Which tailoring step is this?
questions.e: The four steps are: select the initial approach, tailor for the organization, tailor for the project, implement ongoing improvement.

questions.q: A team buys insurance so that a vendor failure would not hurt the project's budget. Which threat strategy is this?
questions.e: Transfer moves the impact and ownership of a threat to a third party, for example through insurance or a contract.

questions.q: Product management and project management are the same thing: both end when the product is delivered.
questions.e: Product management covers the whole product life cycle (introduction, growth, maturity, decline). A project is temporary.

questions.q: Management reserve is part of the cost baseline.
questions.e: The cost baseline includes contingency reserve. Project budget = cost baseline + management reserve.

questions.q: A program is a group of related projects managed together to get benefits that managing them separately would not give.
questions.e: That is the PMBOK definition of a program.

questions.q: In the system for value delivery, leadership shares strategy downward and projects send performance information upward.
questions.e: Information flows both ways: strategy down, performance up.

questions.q: Tailoring means applying the full standard process to every project so results stay consistent.
questions.e: Tailoring is deliberately adapting the approach, governance and processes to fit the environment and the work.

questions.q: Match each performance domain to what it focuses on.
pairs: Productive relationships with the people affected
The cadence and the phases of the work
Assessing performance with metrics and KPIs
Delivering scope and quality that bring outcomes

questions.q: Match each model to the area it helps with.

questions.qc: Put the four steps of the tailoring process in order.
questions.q: Put the four steps of the tailoring process in order. Match each step to its position.

questions.qc: Which development approach fits the project as a whole?
questions.q:
Scenario: MedTrack
A hospital is building a patient app. The billing module must follow fixed national regulations that are fully documented. The AI triage feature uses a model nobody on the team has used before, and doctors are still deciding what it should do.

Which development approach fits the project as a whole?
questions.e: Part of the work is certain (billing) and part is uncertain (AI triage), which is the classic case for a hybrid approach.

questions.qc: Midway through, a new regulation forces work that nobody had identified as a risk. Which reserve normally pays for it?
questions.q:
Scenario: MedTrack
A hospital is building a patient app. The billing module must follow fixed national regulations that are fully documented. The AI triage feature uses a model nobody on the team has used before, and doctors are still deciding what it should do.

Midway through, a new regulation forces work that nobody had identified as a risk. Which reserve normally pays for it?
questions.e: Unplanned, unidentified work is an unknown unknown, so it comes from management reserve.

questions.q: What is the difference between project management and product management?
questions.m: Project management runs a temporary effort that ends when its objective is delivered. Product management looks after the product over its whole life cycle (introduction, growth, maturity, decline) and may start projects at any point.
k: Project: temporary, ends when its objective is met
Product: the whole life cycle of the product

questions.q: Name the four values in the PMI Code of Ethics.
questions.m: Responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty.

questions.q: Define a model, a method and an artifact.
questions.m: A model is a thinking strategy that explains a process or situation. A method is the means of reaching an outcome. An artifact is a template, document or deliverable.
k: Model: a thinking strategy or framework
Method: a means or technique to reach an outcome
Artifact: a template, document or deliverable

questions.q: A PM sets up the plan of audits, reviews and standards before any deliverable is checked. Later, a QA staff member checks one deliverable against those standards, finds a defect and logs a fix. How should each activity be labeled?
o: Setting up the plan is Quality Assurance; checking the deliverable and logging the fix is Quality Control
Setting up the plan is Quality Control; checking the deliverable and logging the fix is Quality Assurance
Both activities are Quality Assurance, because a QA staff member was the person who performed the check
Both activities are Quality Control, because standards and reviews are part of ongoing project monitoring
questions.e: QA builds quality into the process (plans, standards, audits). QC checks results against those standards, whoever performs it.

questions.q: A project finishes on schedule, under budget and meets every signed-off requirement, yet the customer is unhappy. Was it successful?
o: No — customer satisfaction is the real goal; schedule, budget and scope are proxies
Yes — meeting schedule, budget and requirements together automatically means success
Yes — meeting the signed-off requirements always means the product is high quality
No — finishing under budget shows that part of the scope was never fully delivered
questions.e: Schedule, budget and requirements are stand-ins; the customer's satisfaction is what they are meant to predict.

questions.q: A web project has 60 dynamic pages and 15 static pages. What is the customization index C, and what does it say?
o: C = 15 / (60 + 15) = 0.2 — the site is mostly dynamic
C = 60 / (60 + 15) = 0.8 — the site is largely static
C = 60 / 15 = 4.0 — the site is very strongly dynamic
C = 15 / (60 + 15) = 0.2 — the site is largely static
questions.e: C = Nsp ÷ (Ndp + Nsp). A low value means few static pages, so the site is highly customized (dynamic).

questions.q: A retrospective lists “informal, inadequate testing”, “manual design and specification” and “over 30% creep in user requirements”. Which category of factors are these?
o: Risk factors for escalation to the CCB
questions.e: These come from the table of technology factors on unsuccessful projects.

questions.q: Which statement about testing is correct?
o: Testing measures quality but cannot add it
Testing guarantees the product has no defects
Testing replaces the need for a QA process
Testing is needed only for safety software
questions.e: Testing finds defects and measures quality; quality has to be built in by the process.

questions.q: “Lines of code produced per developer-month” is which kind of metric?
questions.e: Size-oriented metrics normalize by size, such as LOC. Function-oriented metrics use function points.

questions.q: Quality assurance focuses on preventing defects through the process.
questions.e: QC finds defects in the results; QA prevents them.

questions.q: Executive support and user involvement are both listed as project success factors.
questions.e: Others include an experienced PM, clear objectives, minimized scope and firm requirements.

questions.q: A process metric tells you about the quality of the delivered product.
questions.e: Product metrics describe the product; process metrics describe how the work is done.

questions.q: Quality control happens only once, at the end of the project.
questions.e: QC monitors results throughout the project against the standards.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A number for one attribute, such as 12 defects
The act of collecting a measure
A measure relating values, such as defects per KLOC
A metric that gives insight into the process or product

questions.qc: What is the customization index C?
questions.q:
Scenario: ShopFast
ShopFast's online store has 48 static pages and 16 dynamic pages. It launched on time and on budget, but customers complain that it does not do what they expected. The team skipped user reviews and the requirements changed weekly.

What is the customization index C?

questions.qc: What does that value of C say about the site?
questions.q:
Scenario: ShopFast
ShopFast's online store has 48 static pages and 16 dynamic pages. It launched on time and on budget, but customers complain that it does not do what they expected. The team skipped user reviews and the requirements changed weekly.

What does that value of C say about the site?
o: Exactly balanced between the two types
Nothing, since C needs function points
questions.e: C near 1 means mostly static pages, so little customization.

questions.qc: Name two success factors from the chapter that ShopFast was clearly missing.
questions.q:
Scenario: ShopFast
ShopFast's online store has 48 static pages and 16 dynamic pages. It launched on time and on budget, but customers complain that it does not do what they expected. The team skipped user reviews and the requirements changed weekly.

Name two success factors from the chapter that ShopFast was clearly missing.
questions.m: User involvement (they skipped user reviews) and firm requirements (they changed every week).

questions.q: What is the difference between quality assurance and quality control?
questions.m: Quality assurance prevents defects by building quality into the process (plans, standards, audits). Quality control monitors the results and checks them against those standards.
k: QA prevents defects through the process (plans, standards, audits)
QC checks the results against the standards

questions.q: Name the four traditional criteria for a successful project.
questions.m: Delivered on schedule, within budget, meeting its requirements, and with high quality.

questions.q: The same developer has owned the payment module for three releases and nobody else understands its code. What kind of risk is this, and what is the best response?
o: Predictable risk → mitigate with cross-training or a reserve
Known risk → avoid it by removing the payment module from scope
Unknowable risk → handle it through crisis or disaster management
Business risk → transfer it to an outside third-party vendor
questions.e: Staff turnover is a predictable risk from past projects. Cross-training, pairing and documentation reduce its impact.

questions.q: The risk that the market rejects the finished product belongs to which category?
questions.e: Business risks threaten the product's viability: market, strategy, sales, management or budget.

questions.q: Legal counsel says the app's data-retention policy may break new regional rules, and the company has no in-house compliance expertise. What is the best classification and response?
o: Business risk → transfer it to hired compliance experts
Technical risk → mitigate it by adding more QA and testing cycles
Business risk → avoid it by dropping the data-retention feature
Business risk → accept it passively, as legal risk is unavoidable
questions.e: It is a legal (business) risk, and contracting outside experts transfers the work to people who can handle it.

questions.q: Hiring an outside expert to reduce a technical risk creates the new risk that the expert leaves mid-project. What is this new risk called?
questions.e: Secondary risks are caused by the response itself. Residual risk is what is left of the original risk.

questions.q: A risk is estimated at 65% probability. Which band of the five-point scale is it in?
questions.e: Likely covers 60–80%. About even is 40–60%; highly likely is above 80%.

questions.q: Experts give anonymous estimates over several rounds, seeing a summary each time, until their answers converge. Which identification technique is this?
questions.e: The Delphi technique uses anonymous rounds so no single voice dominates.

questions.q: A firm puts its best developers on a feature to make sure it earns an early-delivery bonus. Which opportunity strategy is this?
questions.e: Exploit makes sure the opportunity happens. Enhance only raises its probability or impact; share brings in a partner.

questions.q: A risk is an uncertain event that can have either a positive or a negative effect on the project.
questions.e: Negative risks are threats, positive risks are opportunities.

questions.q: Avoiding a risk means reducing its probability or impact.
questions.e: That is mitigation. Avoiding removes the cause, for example by cutting the risky scope.

questions.q: Risk exposure is the probability of the risk multiplied by the size of the loss.
questions.e: RE = P × L, for example 25% × 4 weeks = 1 week.

questions.q: A risk response plan should try to handle every identified risk with the same effort.
questions.e: Use the 80/20 rule and urgency: actively manage the top risks and keep a watch list for the rest.

questions.q: A fallback plan is used when the planned response to a risk does not work.
questions.e: Fallback plans are the backup for responses that fail.

questions.q: Match each threat response to an example.
pairs: Drop the risky feature from scope
Sign a fixed-price contract with a vendor
Add testing to lower the chance of defects
Set aside a contingency reserve and move on

questions.q: Put the risk management process in order. Match each step to its position.

questions.qc: What is the risk exposure of the vendor API risk?
questions.q:
Scenario: CloudCart risks
CloudCart's risk register has three entries:
• Vendor API changes: probability 40%, impact 5 weeks
• A senior developer leaves: probability 20%, impact 8 weeks
• A new privacy law applies: probability 10%, impact 15 weeks

What is the risk exposure of the vendor API risk?

questions.qc: Ranked by exposure, which risk should be handled first?
questions.q:
Scenario: CloudCart risks
CloudCart's risk register has three entries:
• Vendor API changes: probability 40%, impact 5 weeks
• A senior developer leaves: probability 20%, impact 8 weeks
• A new privacy law applies: probability 10%, impact 15 weeks

Ranked by exposure, which risk should be handled first?
questions.e: Exposures: vendor 2.0, developer 1.6, privacy law 1.5 weeks.

questions.qc: For the developer risk, name a response strategy and one concrete action for it.
questions.q:
Scenario: CloudCart risks
CloudCart's risk register has three entries:
• Vendor API changes: probability 40%, impact 5 weeks
• A senior developer leaves: probability 20%, impact 8 weeks
• A new privacy law applies: probability 10%, impact 15 weeks

For the developer risk, name a response strategy and one concrete action for it.
questions.m: Mitigate: cross-train a second developer, pair on the critical code and document it, so losing one person costs much less.
k: A strategy: mitigate, accept or transfer

questions.q: What is the difference between a residual risk and a secondary risk?
questions.m: Residual risk is what is left of the original risk after the response. A secondary risk is a new risk that the response itself creates.
k: Residual: what remains of the risk after the response
Secondary: a new risk caused by the response

questions.q: Name the three risk categories and what each one threatens.
questions.m: Project risks threaten the plan (schedule, cost). Technical risks threaten the quality and timeliness of the software. Business risks threaten the product's viability (market, strategy, sales, budget).
k: Project risk: the plan, schedule or cost
Technical risk: quality or timeliness of the software

questions.q: Activities: A (9 days) and B (3) have no predecessors. C (9) needs B. D (5) needs A and B. E (4) needs A and C. What is the shortest project duration, and which chain is critical?
o: 16 days; critical chain = B → C → E
16 days; critical chain = A → C → E
30 days; critical chain = A → B → C → D → E
questions.e: B→C finishes at day 12; E can start at max(9, 12) = 12 and ends at 16. A→D ends at 14, so B→C→E is critical.

questions.q: A WBS lists “Requirements”, “Analysis”, “Design” and “Testing” at the top level. Which type is it, and who typically uses it?
o: Process WBS (activity-oriented); typically used by the project manager
Product WBS (entity-oriented); typically used by the project manager
Product WBS (entity-oriented); typically used by the engineering manager
Hybrid WBS (phases plus deliverables); used equally by both managers
questions.e: Activities like these make a process WBS, the PM's view. A product WBS lists the things being built.

questions.q: To finish sooner, the team starts coding before the design is fully approved. Which technique is this?
questions.e: Fast-tracking overlaps activities that would normally run in sequence, which adds risk and rework.

questions.q: Where does the critical chain method place a feeding buffer?
o: Where a side chain joins the critical chain
At the very end of the project schedule
At the start of every critical activity
Between each pair of critical activities
questions.e: Feeding buffers protect the critical chain where other chains join it. The project buffer sits at the end.

questions.q: Which of these is a known limitation of a Gantt chart?
o: It does not always show dependencies between tasks
It is hard for most stakeholders to read
It cannot show when each task starts and ends
It cannot be changed once work has started
questions.e: Gantt charts are easy to read and update, but they can hide dependencies and the effect of late starts.

questions.q: According to Brooks's law, what happens when people are added to a late software project?
questions.e: New people need ramp-up time and add communication paths, which slows the team further.

questions.q: Activities on the critical path have zero slack.
questions.e: Any delay to them delays the whole project.

questions.q: Slack can be computed as LS − ES, or equally as LF − EF.
questions.e: Both give the same float.

questions.q: In earned value management, a CPI below 1 means the project is under budget.
questions.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC. Below 1 means more was spent than the work is worth: over budget.

questions.q: A burndown chart plots the work remaining against time.
questions.e: Work remaining on the y-axis, time on the x-axis.

questions.q: Crashing adds resources to activities that are not on the critical path.
questions.e: Crashing adds resources to critical activities; speeding up others gains nothing.

questions.q: Match each earned value measure to its formula.

questions.qc: Put these project control activities in the order they happen.
questions.q: Put these project control activities in the order they happen. Match each step to its position.
PERT: optimistic 2 days, most likely 5 days, pessimistic 14 days. What is the expected time?
PV = 200, EV = 160, AC = 128 hours. What is the CPI?
questions.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 160 ÷ 128 = 1.25 (under budget).

questions.q: Same task: PV = 200, EV = 160, AC = 128 hours. What is the SPI?
questions.e: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 160 ÷ 200 = 0.8 (behind schedule).

questions.qc: What is the minimum project duration?
questions.q:
Scenario: Network diagram
A (3 days) starts the project. B (4) and C (2) both need A. D (5) needs both B and C. E (1) needs D.

What is the minimum project duration?

questions.qc: How much slack does activity C have?
questions.q:
Scenario: Network diagram
A (3 days) starts the project. B (4) and C (2) both need A. D (5) needs both B and C. E (1) needs D.

How much slack does activity C have?
questions.e: C's path is 11 days vs 13 on the critical path, so 2 days of slack.

questions.qc: Which activities are critical?
questions.q:
Scenario: Network diagram
A (3 days) starts the project. B (4) and C (2) both need A. D (5) needs both B and C. E (1) needs D.

Which activities are critical?
questions.e: The longest path is A → B → D → E.

questions.qc: Shortening C by one day would shorten the project by one day.
questions.q:
Scenario: Network diagram
A (3 days) starts the project. B (4) and C (2) both need A. D (5) needs both B and C. E (1) needs D.

Shortening C by one day would shorten the project by one day.
questions.e: C is not critical; its path already has 2 days of slack.

questions.q: Compare crashing and fast-tracking: what does each one do, and what does each one cost?
questions.m: Crashing adds resources to critical-path activities, which costs more money. Fast-tracking runs activities in parallel that were planned in sequence, which adds risk and rework.
k: Crashing adds resources to critical activities

questions.q: What does a process WBS list, and what does a product WBS list?
questions.m: A process WBS lists the activities or phases (the PM's view). A product WBS lists the deliverables and components being built (engineering's view).

questions.q: A regulated safety project has stable requirements and needs formally planned phase gates for its auditors. Which lifecycle fits best?
questions.e: Stable requirements plus formal gates and traceability point to a predictive (waterfall) life cycle.

questions.q: A pipeline automatically deploys every passing change to staging, but a person must approve each release to production. Which practice is this?
questions.e: Continuous delivery keeps every change releasable; production release stays a human decision.

questions.q: On a Scrum team, who is responsible for the team's effectiveness and for removing impediments?
questions.e: The Scrum Master serves the team by coaching and removing impediments.

questions.q: A large, high-risk system needs risk-driven cycles with prototypes before committing more money. Which lifecycle is built for this?
questions.e: Spiral is risk-driven: each loop analyzes risk and often builds a prototype. Its downside is that it is complex to manage.

questions.q: A QA engineer checks that every implemented feature matches the written specification. Which activity is this?
questions.e: Verification asks “did we build the product right?”, meaning against its spec.

questions.q: Which of these is a process rather than a product or a project?
questions.e: A process is a repeatable way of working. The app and release notes are products; building v2 by June is a project.

questions.q: A team tries a new review checklist on one squad for two weeks and collects defect data. Which PDCA step is this?
questions.e: Do runs the experiment on a limited scope and captures evidence. Check compares the results with the hypothesis.

questions.q: Validation asks “did we build the right product?”
questions.e: Validation checks the product is fit for the user's real need.

questions.q: Iterative and incremental development mean the same thing.
questions.e: Iterative refines the product through repeated cycles; incremental adds usable slices one at a time.

questions.q: In continuous deployment, every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically.
questions.e: That missing human gate is what separates it from continuous delivery.

questions.q: Spiral development is a good fit for small, low-risk projects.
questions.e: Its risk-analysis overhead suits large, high-risk projects.

questions.q: Match each software engineering activity to what it does.
pairs: Defines what the system must do and its constraints
Checks the system meets the customer's needs

questions.qc: Put the stages of the CI/CD pipeline in order.
questions.q: Put the stages of the CI/CD pipeline in order. Match each step to its position.

questions.qc: Which practice is the team using?
questions.q:
Scenario: Pipeline review
A startup's pipeline runs automated tests on every commit and deploys passing builds to staging automatically. The product manager approves each production release. The team already tracks lead time.

Which practice is the team using?
questions.e: Automatic staging plus a human production gate is continuous delivery.

questions.qc: If they removed the approval step so every passing build went live, the practice would become continuous deployment.
questions.q:
Scenario: Pipeline review
A startup's pipeline runs automated tests on every commit and deploys passing builds to staging automatically. The product manager approves each production release. The team already tracks lead time.

If they removed the approval step so every passing build went live, the practice would become continuous deployment.
questions.e: Continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically.

questions.qc: Besides lead time, name two of the other DevOps measures.
questions.q:
Scenario: Pipeline review
A startup's pipeline runs automated tests on every commit and deploys passing builds to staging automatically. The product manager approves each production release. The team already tracks lead time.

Besides lead time, name two of the other DevOps measures.
questions.m: Any two of: deployment frequency, change failure rate, time to recover.

questions.q: Distinguish verification from validation.
questions.m: Verification: did we build the product right (does it match its specification)? Validation: did we build the right product (does it meet the user's real needs)?
k: Verification: built the product right / matches the spec
Validation: built the right product / meets user needs

questions.q: Name the three core project constraints.
questions.m: Scope, time (schedule) and cost (budget).

questions.q: Why is iterative development not the same as incremental development?
questions.m: Iterative development refines the product through repeated cycles; incremental development delivers it in usable slices, adding a new piece each time.
k: Iterative: refine the same thing through repeated cycles
Incremental: add new usable slices one at a time

questions.q: A senior finance director controls the project's budget but rarely engages with details and reads only summary reports. Where does this stakeholder sit, and what strategy fits?
o: High power / low interest — keep satisfied with short, relevant updates
High power / high interest — manage closely, involve in key decisions
Low power / high interest — keep informed and invite regular feedback
Low power / low interest — monitor with light, occasional communication
questions.e: Lots of authority, little day-to-day interest: keep satisfied.

questions.q: A frontline support agent has no formal authority but attends every session and gives detailed feedback. Which quadrant and strategy apply?
o: Low power / high interest — keep informed, use as an advocate
High power / high interest — manage closely in key decisions
High power / low interest — keep satisfied with brief updates
Low power / low interest — monitor with minimal communication
questions.e: Little authority but high interest: keep informed.

questions.q: A department head opposes a new workflow because she fears losing control over her team's process. There is time to work it out. Which conflict mode fits best for a lasting agreement?
o: Collaborate — find her underlying concern, then build agreement
Compromise — split the difference quickly, since time is limited
Avoid — leave it alone, since she is only one of many stakeholders
Accommodate — accept her objection right away without discussion
questions.e: With time available, collaborating on the real concern gives the most durable result.

questions.q: A large documentation repository is consulted by many stakeholders, each only when they need something specific. Which communication type fits?
questions.e: Pull suits large audiences who fetch information when needed, such as portals and repositories.

questions.q: A PM wants one document recording who each stakeholder is, an assessment of their interest and influence, and a classification. Which artifact is it?
questions.e: The stakeholder register holds identification, assessment and classification, which is why it needs access control.

questions.q: In the Salience model, a stakeholder with power, urgency and legitimacy is called what?
questions.e: All three attributes make a definitive stakeholder. Dominant has power and legitimacy; dangerous has power and urgency.

questions.q: A stakeholder knows about the project but neither supports nor resists it. Which engagement level is this?
questions.e: The levels run unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading.

questions.q: Push communication includes memos, emails and reports sent to specific people.
questions.e: Push is sent to known recipients; it does not confirm they read it.

questions.q: A web portal that people visit when they need information is interactive communication.
questions.e: That is pull. Interactive is two-way and real time, such as meetings and calls.

questions.q: The stakeholder register can contain sensitive assessments, so access to it should be controlled.
questions.e: It may record frank judgments about people's influence and attitude.

questions.q: Low power, low interest stakeholders should be managed closely.
questions.e: They only need monitoring. High power, high interest stakeholders are managed closely.

What was accomplished in a period
The gap between planned and actual results

questions.q: Team members argue about roles and openly challenge the leader's decisions. Which Tuckman stage is the team in?
questions.e: Storming is the stage of conflict over roles, approach and leadership.

questions.q: A manager settles a dispute by having each developer give up part of what they wanted. Which technique is this?
questions.e: Compromising finds a middle ground where both sides give something up.

questions.q: On a RACI chart, who is the one person who owns the result and signs off on it?
questions.e: Accountable is the single owner who approves the work; Responsible does the work.

questions.q: One expert does the critical design and code, supported by specialists such as a tester and a toolsmith. Which team model is this?
questions.e: The chief programmer (surgical) team is built around one lead expert with supporting roles.

questions.q: The problem has no known solution, so the leader frames questions and gets the team to learn its way forward. Which leadership is this?
questions.e: Adaptive leadership is for problems without a known answer. Technical leadership applies known means, with the leader directing.

questions.q: A developer with a secure, well-paid job now wants her work to be recognized by others. Which need is she trying to meet?
questions.e: Recognition and respect are esteem needs, above social needs in the hierarchy.

questions.q: A team member is driven mainly by personal success and recognition. Which personality type is this?
questions.e: Self-oriented people are motivated by personal success; task-oriented by the work itself; interaction-oriented by the people around them.

questions.q: Vulnerability-based trust means team members are comfortable admitting mistakes and weaknesses to each other.

Adaptive: no known solution, the leader frames questions and mobilizes the team

questions.q: Name three of the steps for reaching consensus.

questions.q: A developer gets daily priorities from a project manager but performance reviews from the head of engineering, and the two keep giving conflicting instructions. Which structure is this, and which weakness is showing?

Project; loyalty to the project over the firm
Matrix; it makes the most of scarce resources
questions.e: Reporting to both a functional manager and a project manager is the matrix's dual hierarchy, and conflicting orders are its main weakness.

questions.q: A company uses its strong engineering team to move into a fast-growing market. Which SWOT strategy is this?
questions.e: Using a strength (S) to take an opportunity (O) is the SO, or Maxi-Maxi, strategy.

questions.q: A PMO offers templates, training and best practices, but has little control over how projects are run. Which form is it?
questions.e: Supportive PMOs have low control, controlling PMOs moderate control, directive PMOs high control.

questions.q: A PMO keeps a group of trained project managers and loans them out to projects across the company. Which PMO model is this?
questions.e: The resource pool model maintains and assigns project managers. A weather station only tracks and reports; a control tower sets and enforces standards.

questions.q: An environmental group campaigns against a new mining-software project. What kind of stakeholder is it?
questions.e: Intervenor groups are outside parties, such as activists or regulators, who can step in and affect a project.

questions.q: Which of these is a strength of the pure project structure?
o: Makes efficient use of scarce resources
Causes no disruption to the firm's design
questions.e: With one PM holding full authority, a project organization decides and reacts quickly. The other three are strengths of the functional or matrix forms.

questions.q: Lockheed's Skunk Works is the classic example of which kind of organization?
questions.e: Heavyweight organizations give a dedicated team full authority, often in a separate location, to work fast.

questions.q: In a functional structure, project work causes little disruption to the firm's design.
questions.e: Projects stay inside existing departments, so the structure does not change. The cost is silos and slow responses.

questions.q: A directive PMO has the lowest level of control over projects.
questions.e: Directive PMOs have the highest control; supportive PMOs have the lowest.

questions.q: Projects are one of the main ways an organization puts its strategy into action.
questions.e: Projects reflect and carry out strategy, which is why selection should follow strategic goals.

questions.q: In a pure project structure, the project manager shares authority over the team with functional managers.
questions.e: In a project structure the PM has sole authority. Shared authority is the matrix.

questions.q: Match each structure to its main weakness.
pairs: Silos and slow responses across departments
Costly set-up and loyalty to the project, not the firm
Two bosses and conflict over shared staff

questions.q: Match each culture item to whether it is a factor that shapes culture or an effect culture has on projects.
questions.e: Factors: technology, environment, location, reward systems, rules, key members. Effects: departmental interaction, employee commitment, project planning, performance evaluation.

questions.qc: Which structure does NovaSoft use today?
