Scenario: NovaSoft
NovaSoft's developers belong to departments (backend, mobile, QA) and are borrowed by projects as needed. Leadership now needs a new product in four months to beat a competitor, and is considering moving six engineers to a separate office under one leader with full authority over the work.

Which structure does NovaSoft use today?
questions.e: Staff stay in their departments but are loaned to projects, which is a matrix.

questions.qc: What kind of team is leadership considering?
questions.q:
Scenario: NovaSoft
NovaSoft's developers belong to departments (backend, mobile, QA) and are borrowed by projects as needed. Leadership now needs a new product in four months to beat a competitor, and is considering moving six engineers to a separate office under one leader with full authority over the work.

What kind of team is leadership considering?
questions.e: A dedicated, separate team with full authority is a heavyweight, or skunk works, team.

questions.qc: Give one advantage and one risk of the separate team.
questions.q:
Scenario: NovaSoft
NovaSoft's developers belong to departments (backend, mobile, QA) and are borrowed by projects as needed. Leadership now needs a new product in four months to beat a competitor, and is considering moving six engineers to a separate office under one leader with full authority over the work.

Give one advantage and one risk of the separate team.
questions.m: Advantage: decisions are fast and the team is fully focused. Risk: it is expensive, and the team can become isolated or loyal to the project instead of the company, which makes it hard to bring them back.

questions.q: Name the three PMO forms and say how much control each one has.
questions.m: Supportive (low control), controlling (moderate control) and directive (high control).

questions.q: List four factors that shape an organization's culture.
questions.m: Any four of: technology, environment, geographic location, reward systems, rules and procedures, key organizational members.

questions.q: Define the term ‘project constraints’ and explain how they influence project planning and execution. Provide at least three examples of common constraints and discuss their interrelationship.
questions.m: Project constraints are the limits a project must be delivered within. The classic three are scope, time and cost, often with quality, resources and risk. They drive planning because every schedule, budget and scope decision has to fit inside them, and during execution the PM keeps trading them off. They are interrelated (the triple constraint): cutting the schedule usually needs more cost or less scope, and adding scope needs more time or money; quality sits in the middle and suffers if they are squeezed.

questions.q: Explain what is a Gantt chart and describe its significance in planning and tracking project activities. In your answer, define the terms milestone and dependency, and provide one example of each as they would appear in a Gantt chart.
questions.m: A Gantt chart is a bar chart with activities down the side and a time scale across, where each bar shows an activity's start, finish and duration. It makes the schedule easy to read for planning (sequence, overlaps, who works when) and for tracking, because actual progress is shaded against the planned bars. A milestone is a significant point or event with zero duration, shown as a diamond, e.g. “Requirements signed off”. A dependency is a logical relationship where one activity can't start (or finish) until another does, shown as an arrow, e.g. “Coding” can't start until “Design approved” finishes (finish-to-start).

questions.q: What is a Project Management Office (PMO) and its role in organizations?
questions.m: A PMO is a centralized organizational unit that oversees and standardizes how projects are managed. It sets PM standards, methods and templates, trains and supports project managers, monitors and reports on project performance, and coordinates resources across projects. Its control ranges from supportive (consultative) to controlling (requires compliance) to directive (manages the projects directly).

questions.q: As the project manager, you must ensure that the 12-month development timeline is realistic and achievable. Identify three project scheduling methods/techniques you would use to plan the sequence and timing of tasks. Briefly explain how each method helps in identifying delays or managing overlapping activities.
questions.m: 1) Network diagram + Critical Path Method: shows dependencies and the longest path; any delay on a zero-slack critical activity delays the whole project, while slack shows how much other tasks can slip. 2) Gantt chart: shows each task on a timeline, so overlapping activities, resource clashes and slipping bars (actual vs planned) are easy to spot. 3) PERT: uses optimistic, most-likely and pessimistic durations ((O + 4M + P) / 6), useful for uncertain design, prototyping and regulatory work, so likely delays are built in.

questions.q: You are responsible for managing a diverse team with varying availability and skill sets. Describe two strategies you would use to allocate your team’s resources efficiently across tasks. How would you adjust your resource plan if one hardware specialist becomes unavailable for 4 weeks?
questions.m: 1) Use a skills matrix and RAM to assign work by skill and availability, so specialists only do work that needs them. 2) Use resource leveling (and a resource histogram) to remove overallocation, shifting non-critical tasks within their slack. If a hardware specialist is out for 4 weeks: move their non-critical tasks inside their float, give critical tasks to the other three specialists (cross-training if needed) or bring in a temporary contractor, then update the schedule and tell the stakeholders the impact.

questions.q: You are estimating the effort required to develop the monitoring software for the smart solar panel system. Based on the COCOMO model for an Organic project: size 32 KLOC; a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38. Calculate the estimated effort in person-months, development time and average staff size for the project.

As the project manager for the smart solar panel system, you’re expected to manage risks proactively throughout the 12-month development cycle. Describe two techniques you would use during the planning phase to identify and document project risks. Explain how a Risk Assessment Matrix helps in making informed decisions about which risks need immediate action.
questions.m: Brainstorming with engineers, hardware specialists and developers, and expert interviews / Delphi with people who have done regulatory approvals, both recorded in a risk register (risk, cause, owner, response). A checklist from past projects also works. The Risk Assessment Matrix plots each risk's probability against its impact; the score ranks the risks, so high-probability, high-impact (red) risks get immediate responses and owners, medium ones are planned for, and low ones are just monitored.

questions.q: How does the stakeholder management process contribute to the success of a project? Identify two inputs, techniques and outputs of the stakeholder management process, and explain their role in ensuring effective stakeholder management.
questions.m: Stakeholder management identifies everyone affected, understands their interests and influence, and keeps them engaged, so the project gains support, catches conflicting expectations early and avoids late resistance. Inputs: the project charter (who sponsors and is affected) and enterprise environmental factors / organizational process assets (culture, past registers). Techniques: stakeholder analysis with a power/interest grid or salience model (prioritize who needs the most attention) and meetings with interpersonal skills (build relationships). Outputs: the stakeholder register (who they are, their interest, influence and engagement level) and the stakeholder engagement plan (how each one will be engaged and communicated with).

questions.q: Calculate the number of communication channels for a project team of 7 members.
Identify all the paths on the network diagram and calculate how long they are.
What is the minimum completion time of this project?
questions.m: 26, the length of the critical path A-D-E-F-G-H.

questions.q: In the context of the Team Needs Pyramid, explain how a project manager can foster commitment among team members.
questions.m: In the pyramid (trust → managed conflict → commitment → accountability → results), commitment sits on trust and healthy conflict: people commit when they trust each other and have had their say. The PM fosters it with clarity (clear decisions, goals, roles and deadlines, confirmed at the end of each meeting) and buy-in (letting everyone voice their views so they support the decision even if they disagreed; consensus isn't required).

questions.q: How does fostering trust and managing conflict within a software project team contribute to improved collaboration and project success?
questions.m: Trust lets members admit mistakes, share information and ask for help, so problems surface early and people cooperate instead of protecting themselves. Managed (healthy) conflict means ideas are debated openly and respectfully, which gives better technical decisions and avoids groupthink or disputes that turn personal. Together they lead to real commitment and collaboration, which drives quality and project success.

questions.q: Your software project team is experiencing delays due to unclear task ownership and inconsistent updates. As the project manager, how would you apply a team-based approach to improve accountability and transparency within the team? Describe specific steps you would take to enhance collaboration and increase the project’s chances of success.
questions.m: 1) Clarify ownership with a RACI matrix so every task has one Responsible and one Accountable person. 2) Hold short daily stand-ups (done, next, blocked) so updates are consistent. 3) Put all tasks on a shared board (e.g. Jira or Kanban) with visible goals and deadlines so progress is transparent. 4) Encourage peer accountability and run retrospectives to fix what caused the delays.

questions.q: How can the use of crashing and fast-tracking affect the overall project cost and risk?
questions.m: Crashing shortens critical-path activities by adding resources (people, overtime, equipment). It raises cost, often with diminishing returns, and adds coordination risk. Fast-tracking overlaps activities that would normally run in sequence. It adds little direct cost but raises risk, because work starts on incomplete inputs and may need rework.

questions.q: How can a burn chart help a project manager track progress and identify if the team is ahead or behind schedule?
questions.m: A burndown chart plots the work remaining (e.g. story points) against time, next to an ideal line from the total down to zero at the end of the sprint. If the actual line is above the ideal line the team is behind; below it, ahead. A burnup chart shows completed work rising toward the scope line and also reveals scope changes. Either one gives an early warning, so the PM can act (remove blockers, re-prioritize, adjust scope) before the deadline.

questions.q: In decentralized project management, decision-making authority is primarily:
o: Distributed among team members to encourage shared accountability.
Concentrated in the hands of a single project manager.
Transferred to external auditors for oversight.
Reserved exclusively for senior executives in the organization.
questions.e: Decentralized management spreads decisions across the team; centralized puts them with one person such as the PM.

questions.q: A group of related projects managed in a coordinated manner to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually is called a:
questions.e: A program is related projects managed together for benefits; a portfolio groups projects, programs and operations for strategic objectives and they can be unrelated.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains the nature of project performance domains?
o: They represent distinct areas of focus that guide effective project management.
They are rigid processes that must be followed in order, from initiation to closure.
They are optional tools that project managers may use only in large projects.
They are specific deliverables required at the end of each project phase.
questions.e: Performance domains are groups of related activities (areas of focus) that run concurrently; they are not sequential processes or deliverables.

questions.q: In project management, what is the primary purpose of establishing a project cadence?
o: To create a predictable rhythm that supports coordination, communication, and timely delivery.
To enforce strict deadlines that cannot be adjusted under any circumstances.
To eliminate the need for stakeholder engagement during development.
To ensure that all deliverables are produced only at the end of the project.
questions.e: Cadence is the rhythm of activities (single, multiple, periodic or continuous delivery) that keeps the work coordinated.

questions.q: Which of the following best reflects the principle of “Stewardship” in project management?
o: Delegating all responsibility for ethical practices to external auditors
Taking personal responsibility for the careful use of resources, upholding values, and acting with integrity.
Focusing only on delivering project outputs, regardless of long-term impacts.
Ensuring accountability is limited to the project sponsor alone.
questions.e: Stewardship means acting with integrity, care, trustworthiness and compliance, inside and outside the organization.

questions.q: In which type of project would an iterative development approach be most beneficial?
o: A project where requirements are unclear and expected to evolve over time.
A project with well-defined, unchanging requirements from the start.
A project that must deliver the entire product only at final completion.
A project that cannot accommodate stakeholder feedback during execution.
questions.e: Iterative development refines ideas through feedback, which suits unclear or evolving requirements.

questions.q: According to Tuckman’s model of team development, which stage is characterized by members competing for leadership and struggling with group processes?
questions.e: Storming is when members compete for leadership and test group processes; norming comes after, when agreement is reached.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered the foundation of teamwork?
questions.e: Trust is the base of the team pyramid: trust, managed conflict, commitment, accountability, results.

questions.q: In the context of the “system for value delivery,” which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Only portfolios and programs contribute to value delivery in an organization, while projects and products have no significant role.
A system for value delivery includes portfolios, programs, projects, products, and operations, all working together to build, sustain, or advance an organization.
Value delivery systems are only relevant to large organizations and do not apply to small businesses.
Products are the sole contributor to value delivery, with programs and projects serving as support.
questions.e: The value delivery system is the whole set of portfolios, programs, projects, products and operations working together.

questions.q: In a cohesive team, which of the following is an advantage?
o: Members avoid challenging each other’s work to reduce conflict.
Group quality standards can be developed and maintained collectively.
Each member works independently without needing oversight.
Decision-making is always faster due to consensus.
questions.e: Cohesive groups can set and keep shared quality standards, learn from each other and practise egoless programming. Avoiding challenge is groupthink, a risk of cohesion.

questions.q: What are key characteristics of a good team?
questions.m: A good team trusts each other enough to speak openly and admit mistakes, shares a clear goal with clear roles, debates ideas in healthy conflict, commits to decisions, holds each other accountable, and puts team results ahead of individual credit.

questions.q: What does vulnerability-based trust involve?
questions.m: Team members are comfortable being open with each other: admitting mistakes and weaknesses, asking for help, and saying “I don't know”, without fear that it will be used against them. It is the foundation of the team pyramid.

questions.q: Why is healthy conflict important in teams?
questions.m: Healthy conflict is open debate about ideas, not people. It brings out different perspectives so the team makes better decisions, avoids groupthink and artificial harmony, and surfaces problems early. Because everyone has been heard, members are more willing to commit to the final decision even if they disagreed.

questions.q: What’s the difference between a Business Team and a Democratic Team?
questions.m: A business team has a technical lead who is the principal contact and makes or facilitates decisions, with the other members at equal status under the lead (a strong or loose hierarchy). A democratic team acts as a group: decisions are made by consensus, the leader is only the external interface, tasks are allocated by ability and experience, and it works best with experienced, competent members.

questions.q: How can a project manager balance technical leadership with adaptive leadership in a software team?
questions.m: First diagnose the problem. When it can be solved by known means (a coding standard, an architecture choice the PM knows well), use technical leadership: give direction from expertise and vision. When it can't (new technology, unclear requirements), use adaptive leadership: frame the purpose, ask questions, let the team experiment and learn, and motivate through visible progress. Switching between the two as the situation changes is the balance.

questions.q: Your team has been assigned to develop a mobile app for a local fitness center. The app will allow users to book classes, track workouts, and receive personalized fitness tips. The project is expected to be completed in 8 weeks. Fill in the RACI assignments for T1 and T6 only. Assign one or more roles to each task: R = Responsible (does the work), A = Accountable (owns the outcome), C = Consulted (provides input), I = Informed (kept updated).
questions.m: These cells come from the instructor's key. The person who does the work is R (the client representative for requirements, the UI/UX designer for the interface, the lead developer for building and launching, the marketing specialist for promotion). Whoever's expertise is needed is C, and everyone else is I. The key makes the PM Accountable (A) for requirements and launch, the two tasks that commit the project; on the other tasks the PM is kept Informed.

questions.q: During a sprint deployment, a key feature was discovered to be not thoroughly tested and caused issues after release. As the project manager, what steps would you follow to address this issue and ensure accountability within the team?
questions.m: Use a RACI matrix to establish who was Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for testing that feature (0.5). Hold a retrospective to find the root cause (0.25). Make the responsible roles clear without blaming individuals (0.25). Take corrective action: release a hotfix, redistribute tasks, and add automated testing so it can't recur (0.25). Inform the stakeholders of the recovery plan (0.25).

questions.q: Given the evolving requirements (student usability, advisor requests, IT integration rules), which development approach (Agile, Waterfall, or Hybrid) would you recommend, and why would it be the best fit for this project?
questions.m: Agile (Scrum) (0.5), because it handles the evolving requirements from students, advisors and IT, delivers iteratively so each sprint gets feedback, and integrates with DevOps pipelines for frequent tested releases (0.5).

questions.q: Identify three main stakeholder groups for this project, describe their roles, and explain how their input will shape the system.
questions.m: Students are the end users; their input shapes usability and flexibility (0.3). The IT/portal team ensures integration, security and compliance with the university’s IT policies (0.3). Faculty advisors and administration ensure study-plan rules are enforced and use the system to monitor students (0.4).

questions.q: As the project manager, you must establish the team structure for this project. What team structure would you create to ensure smooth development, stakeholder engagement, and integration with the student portal, and why?
questions.m: A cross-functional Agile team: a Project Manager, a Product Owner from the portal/IT team, developers, a UI/UX designer, QA testers, a faculty advisor representative and a student representative (1.0). This puts every stakeholder's voice inside the team, balances usability against compliance, and supports iterative delivery (0.5).

questions.q: What’s the best time to reinforce accountability?
questions.m: As early and as often as possible: make expectations and commitments clear and public at the start, then address a missed commitment immediately when it happens instead of waiting for the end-of-project review, and keep reinforcing it in regular progress reviews where peers hold each other accountable.

questions.q: How does project management contribute to organizations in achieving their strategic objectives? Please elaborate.
questions.m: Strategy is carried out through projects. Project management selects and prioritizes projects (through portfolios and programs) so they align with strategic objectives, then delivers them so the outputs create the intended outcomes, benefits and value. It uses limited resources efficiently, controls scope, time and cost, and manages risk and change. That lets the organization reach its goals and respond to its market faster than competitors.

questions.q: What are the key distinctions between project management and general management, particularly concerning their respective focuses, skill sets, and approaches to managing teams and resources?
questions.m: Focus: project management delivers temporary, unique work with a defined start, end and scope; general management runs the ongoing, repetitive operations of a function. Skills: a PM needs planning, scheduling, risk, stakeholder and integration skills across functions; a general manager needs depth in one function and long-term operational skills. Teams and resources: a PM leads a temporary, cross-functional team, often borrowed from functional managers, so works by influence and negotiation within a fixed budget and schedule; a general manager has permanent staff, line authority and an ongoing departmental budget.

questions.q: Describe the significance of a project scope statement in project management and elaborate on how it aids in mitigating project risks and ensuring successful project outcomes.
questions.m: The scope statement defines what the project will and won't deliver: objectives, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, assumptions and constraints. It reduces risk because everyone agrees on the boundaries up front, it's the baseline for change control (so scope creep is caught and evaluated rather than absorbed), and it's the basis for the WBS, estimates and schedule. That leads to realistic plans and a result the stakeholders will accept.

questions.q: Give an example of a project management tool or technique that you might use to manage a complex software development project, and explain how it could help you ensure project success.
questions.m: A Work Breakdown Structure: it decomposes the complex system into smaller deliverables and work packages that can be estimated, assigned and tracked. Nothing is forgotten, ownership is clear, and the WBS is the base for the schedule, budget and risk analysis, so problems show up early and progress is measurable. (Other valid answers: Gantt chart, CPM, risk register, Scrum board with a burndown chart, each with its benefit explained.)

questions.q: What software estimation techniques would you use to estimate the time and effort required to complete the project, and why? How would you validate your estimates?
questions.m: Function points (or story points with planning poker) sized from the detailed requirements list: dashboards, reorder alerts, multi-store sync and role security are countable functions. Then three-point (PERT) estimates per feature to capture uncertainty, especially for multi-store synchronization. Validate by comparing the two methods and historical data from similar projects, having the developers review the estimates, and tracking actual velocity in the first sprints to re-estimate.

questions.q: How would you go about resourcing the project, taking into account the skills and availability of your team members, as well as any potential risks or constraints?
questions.m: Build a skills matrix for the four developers, the UX designer and the QA analyst, and assign work with a RAM/RACI so each feature has a clear owner who has the right skills. Check everyone's availability per sprint and level the workload so no one is overallocated. Plan for risks: the single UX designer and single QA analyst are bottlenecks and key-person risks, so cross-train developers to help test, keep a schedule buffer, and agree escalation for extra resources.

questions.q: What scheduling techniques would you use to create a realistic timeline for the project, and how would you ensure that you stay on track throughout the development process?
questions.m: Break the work down with a WBS, sequence it in a network diagram to find the critical path, and lay it out as a release plan of sprints across the five months on a Gantt chart with milestones. Include a buffer for integration and testing. To stay on track, use burndown charts and daily stand-ups within sprints, review milestones against the baseline, and re-plan or re-prioritize the backlog as soon as variance appears.

questions.q: List any 2 software risk identification techniques and explain how would you mitigate potential risks that could impact the success of the project? How would you prioritize and monitor these risks throughout the project lifecycle?
questions.m: Identify risks by brainstorming with the team and by using a checklist from past cloud projects (or expert interviews / Delphi). Mitigate them with planned responses, e.g. prototype multi-store synchronization early, add automated testing for the reorder logic, transfer hosting risk to the cloud provider's SLA, and keep contingency time. Prioritize each risk by probability × impact on a risk matrix, record it in a risk register with an owner and trigger, and review the register every sprint.

questions.q: A software project with 20 KLOC is being developed using the organic mode of COCOMO (a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38). Calculate the effort, development time, productivity, and staff required for this project.
questions.m: E = 2.4 × 20^1.05 = 2.4 × 23.23 ≈ 55.76 person-months. TDEV = 2.5 × 55.76^0.38 ≈ 2.5 × 4.61 ≈ 11.52 months. Productivity = size ÷ E = 20,000 ÷ 55.76 ≈ 358.7 LOC per person-month (0.359 KLOC/PM). Staff = E ÷ TDEV = 55.76 ÷ 11.52 ≈ 4.84, about 5 people. The paper doesn't print the constants; these are the standard organic values from the slides.

questions.q: In what ways do proficient communication abilities contribute to the management of project risks and the attainment of project success? Illustrate with an instance of how a breakdown in communication could affect a project, and propose methods for prevention or resolution.
questions.m: Good communication surfaces risks and issues early so they can be handled while they are cheap, keeps requirements and expectations shared across the team and stakeholders, and supports fast, informed decisions, all of which drive success. Example: the backend team changes an API without telling the frontend team; integration fails at the end of the sprint, causing rework, a missed release and an unhappy client. Prevention: a communication plan (who needs what, how often, which channel), daily stand-ups, documented decisions in one shared place, and change notifications. Resolution: an immediate joint meeting, active listening to clarify the misunderstanding, confirming the agreed interface in writing, and updating the plan and stakeholders.

questions.q: How can project managers identify and prioritize stakeholders, and what strategies can they use to communicate effectively with each stakeholder group?
questions.m: Identify stakeholders by brainstorming with the team, reading the charter and contracts, and interviewing key people, then record them in a stakeholder register. Prioritize them with a power/interest grid (or the salience model: power, legitimacy, urgency). Then tailor communication: high power and high interest → manage closely with interactive meetings; high power, low interest → keep satisfied with concise push reports; low power, high interest → keep informed with push updates or pull (portal); low/low → monitor.

questions.q: Imagine that you are the project manager for a software development project. Describe the steps you would take to develop a project plan that incorporates basic project management principles. How would you ensure that the plan is communicated effectively to all stakeholders?
questions.m: Define the objectives and scope with the stakeholders (charter and scope statement); break the work into a WBS; estimate effort and durations; build the schedule (network diagram, critical path, Gantt); assign resources and set the budget; then add a risk plan, a quality plan and a communication plan, applying principles such as stakeholder engagement, value focus and tailoring. Communicate it through a kickoff meeting, a version of the plan tailored to each stakeholder group, a shared location everyone can access, and regular status updates with a way to give feedback.

questions.q: Share an experience from a software project you were involved in where collaboration among team members significantly contributed to its success. Describe the specific strategies or techniques you employed to foster collaboration.
questions.m: Any honest experience earns marks if it names concrete techniques. For example: in a course project building a booking app, we split the work by feature with clear owners, met twice a week for short stand-ups, tracked tasks on a shared Trello board, used GitHub pull requests so every change was reviewed by a teammate, and paired up on the hardest integration work. Decisions were discussed openly, so everyone committed to them, and we delivered on time.

questions.q: You are leading a cross-functional team tasked with selecting a continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) platform for an upcoming project. The team includes software developers, DevOps engineers, and QA testers, each with distinct expectations regarding automation workflows and pipeline management. Describe your approach to collaboratively choosing the most suitable CI/CD platform. Explain how you would involve all team members in the decision-making process and specify the criteria you would apply to evaluate different CI/CD solutions.
questions.m: Run a kickoff workshop where developers, DevOps engineers and QA testers each list their needs (build speed, deployment control, test automation), then agree the criteria and their weights together: integration with our repository and tools, automation and test support, pipeline flexibility, scalability and performance, security, cost, ease of use, and vendor/community support. Shortlist two or three platforms, run a short pilot or proof of concept with members from every role, score each platform on the weighted matrix, and discuss the results openly so the final choice has everyone's buy-in.

questions.q: Your team has just completed a major milestone in the project development process. How would you celebrate this achievement collaboratively with your team members? How would you recognize individual contributions to the team’s success? What actions would you take to ensure that team morale remains high as you move forward in the project?
questions.m: Celebrate as a team, e.g. a team lunch and an announcement of the milestone to the stakeholders. Recognize individuals specifically and publicly: name what each person contributed in the meeting, send thank-you notes to their managers, and give certificates or small rewards. Keep morale high with a retrospective that captures what went well, clear and achievable next goals, a balanced workload to avoid burnout, growth opportunities, and continued recognition, not only at milestones.

questions.q: What does a burndown chart measure, and how are its two axes labeled in Agile project management?
questions.m: It measures the work remaining against time, showing whether the team will finish on schedule. X-axis: time (days of the sprint, or sprints/iterations). Y-axis: work remaining (story points, hours or tasks).

questions.q: What is a Gantt chart, and what does it show in project management?
questions.m: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart of the project's activities against a time scale. It shows each task's start and finish dates and duration, the overlaps and dependencies between tasks, the milestones, and the progress made.

questions.q: What are two advantages of using a Gantt chart?
questions.m: 1) It's visual and easy to understand, so it communicates the schedule well to the team and stakeholders. 2) It helps plan and track: overlaps, dependencies and deadlines are visible, and actual progress can be compared with the plan.

questions.q: A team adds automated regression tests so that a known integration defect is less likely to reach production. Which risk response strategy is the team using?
questions.e: Mitigate reduces the probability or impact of a threat; the defect can still happen, just less likely.

questions.q: Two companies agree to bid together on a large government contract that neither could win alone, splitting the work and the profit. Which opportunity strategy is this?
questions.e: Share brings in a third party to capture an opportunity the organization can't capture alone.

questions.q: A project manager discovers a legal risk that affects several projects in the company and is outside the PM's authority to decide. What should the PM do?
o: Accept the risk and record it in the log
Escalate the risk to senior management
Transfer the risk to the project team
Mitigate it within the project budget
questions.e: Escalate is used when a threat or opportunity is outside the project's scope or the PM's authority.

questions.q: A small internal tool is built with a short charter and a single weekly review, while the company's large regulated projects use full documentation and formal gates. Which principle does this show?
questions.e: Tailoring designs a 'just enough' approach that fits the project's size, criticality and environment.

questions.q: A project manager reports a budget overrun honestly to the sponsor and makes sure the project keeps meeting the regulations it must follow. Which principle is most directly demonstrated?
questions.e: Stewardship means acting responsibly with integrity, care, trustworthiness and compliance.

questions.q: A key vendor goes out of business mid-project. The team quickly reorganizes the work, finds a replacement, and recovers within two weeks. Which principle does this show?
o: Enable change to achieve the envisioned future state
Recognize, evaluate, and respond to system interactions
questions.e: Resiliency is absorbing an impact and recovering quickly from a setback; adaptability is responding to changed conditions.

questions.q: During a crisis, a developer with no formal title organizes the team's response and keeps everyone motivated. Which principle does this illustrate?
o: Create a collaborative project team environment
Be a diligent, respectful, and caring steward
questions.e: Leadership is different from authority: any team member can demonstrate leadership behaviors.

questions.q: The customer expects requirements to change often and wants to see working features every two weeks so they can give feedback. Which development approach fits best?
questions.e: Adaptive approaches suit uncertain, volatile requirements: a clear vision first, then requirements refined from feedback in short iterations with demos.

questions.q: A hospital project builds a new wing (requirements fixed by safety codes) and, in parallel, a patient mobile app whose features will evolve from user feedback. Which approach describes the whole project?
questions.e: Hybrid combines predictive and adaptive elements, useful when deliverables can be modularized or built by different teams.

questions.q: A team builds a rough prototype, shows it to users, and reworks it several times to clarify what the requirements actually are. Which development style is this?
o: Incremental: adding finished features one release at a time
Iterative: repeating ideas to clarify scope and approach
Predictive: defining all requirements before building
questions.e: Iterative development tries different ideas and refines them through feedback to clarify scope, approach and requirements.

questions.q: An estimate is built from a detailed line-by-line breakdown of every task, yet the project ends up costing twice the estimate. How should this estimate be described?
questions.e: Precision is exactness and level of detail; accuracy is correctness, i.e. closeness to the actual result.

questions.q: Midway through the project, unplanned in-scope work appears that nobody had identified as a risk. Which reserve should normally pay for it?
o: Contingency reserve, held by the project manager
Management reserve, held by upper management
The cost baseline, held by the project team
The procurement budget, held by purchasing
questions.e: Management reserve covers unknown events and unplanned in-scope work; it sits above the cost baseline and is usually controlled by upper management, the sponsor, or the PMO.

questions.q: A company knows the exact specifications of the 200 servers it needs and wants vendors' best price and delivery date. Which bid document should it issue?
questions.e: An RFQ asks for price and timeline when the item is fully specified.

questions.q: A project manager tracks the weekly rate of scope change requests to spot schedule trouble before it happens. What kind of measure is this?
questions.e: Leading indicators are proactive and predict changes or trends, e.g. rate of scope change requests.

questions.q: To make a large system easier to manage, the team splits it into independent services so each can be understood and changed on its own. Which way of handling complexity is this?
questions.e: Decoupling (systems-based) disconnects parts of a system to simplify it and reduce connected variables.

questions.q: The team has three equally reasonable architectures to choose from and cannot tell which one will turn out best. What is this?
questions.e: Situational ambiguity is when more than one outcome or option is possible.

questions.q: A team picks Scrum, then adds a monthly report because the company's PMO requires one from every project. Which tailoring step is the monthly report?
questions.e: Tailoring for the organization aligns the chosen approach with organizational governance, policies and required controls.

questions.q: Before starting, a PM wants to judge how uncertain the requirements and technology are in order to choose waterfall, agile, or hybrid. Which model helps most?
questions.e: The Stacey matrix helps decide whether to use waterfall, agile, or hybrid.

questions.q: Which of the following is an artifact rather than a model or a method?
questions.e: An artifact is a template, document, output or deliverable; a risk register is a log/register artifact.

questions.q: A developer receives conflicting instructions from the head of engineering and from the project manager for the same week. Which organizational structure, and which weakness, does this show?
o: Project structure: team loyal to project over firm
Matrix structure: dual hierarchy with two bosses
Matrix structure: it maximizes scarce resources
questions.e: A matrix creates a dual hierarchy, so workers have two bosses and get caught between project and functional demands.

questions.q: A PMO requires every project to use the same status-report template and follow the company's PM standards, but it does not run the projects itself. Which PMO form is this?
questions.e: A controlling PMO has moderate control and requires compliance with adopted PM standards and processes.

questions.q: A company with strong in-house cloud skills sees rising demand for cloud migration services and launches projects to win that market. Which TOWS strategy is this?
questions.e: SO uses internal strengths to maximize external opportunities.

questions.q: Because lateness is publicly criticized, team members routinely double their task estimates. Which effect of organizational culture on project management is this?
questions.e: Culture affects project planning: people pad estimates where lateness is punished; a culture of trust gives honest estimates.

questions.q: Under a looming deadline, the PM ends a long debate by deciding the solution herself and telling the team to implement it. Which conflict-resolution technique is this?
questions.e: Forcing imposes a solution through authority or pressure.

questions.q: A team has argued about roles for weeks but has now agreed how it will make decisions and share work. Which Tuckman stage has it reached?
questions.e: Norming is when agreement is reached on how the group operates.

questions.q: Team members follow a PM's direction mainly because they respect her deep knowledge of the system's architecture. Which type of influence is she using?
questions.e: Expert influence is based on specialized knowledge or skills.

questions.q: The project faces a problem nobody has solved before, and the known best practices don't apply. What kind of leadership is needed?
o: Technical leadership, driven by the leader's vision
Adaptive leadership, driven by shared purpose
Autocratic leadership, to speed up every decision
No leadership, since the team should self-organize
questions.e: Adaptive leadership mobilizes people to solve problems that cannot be solved by known means, through learning, good questions and clarity of purpose.

questions.q: The principles of project management are prescriptive rules that must be followed in a fixed way.
questions.e: They are not prescriptive; they guide behavior, and how they are applied depends on context.

questions.q: Project performance domains run concurrently throughout the project, regardless of how value is delivered.
questions.e: Domains are interactive, interrelated and interdependent, and run at the same time.

questions.q: Management activities may be centralized or distributed, but leadership activities should be practiced by all team members.
questions.e: That is exactly how the Team domain separates management from leadership.

questions.q: Product management covers a product across its whole life cycle, while a project is a temporary endeavor that may create or improve that product.
questions.e: Product management may start projects at any point in the product life cycle; each project has a beginning and an end.

questions.q: Contingency reserve is used for unknown events that nobody identified as risks.
questions.e: Contingency reserve covers identified risks; management reserve covers unknown, unplanned in-scope work.

questions.q: Tailoring is done once at the start of a project and then left alone.
questions.e: Implement ongoing improvement is the fourth step: review points, phase gates and retrospectives keep tailoring going.

questions.q: A weather-station PMO directly manages projects and their project managers.
questions.e: A weather station only monitors and tracks; a directive PMO is the one that manages projects directly.

questions.q: In a project organization, each project is a self-contained unit with a dedicated team assigned for as long as it is needed.
questions.e: That is the defining feature of the project structure.

questions.q: Buy-in requires every team member to fully agree with a decision.
questions.e: Buy-in does not require consensus: members can disagree and still commit because they trust the process.

questions.q: Accountability on a strong team happens directly among peers, not only through the manager.
questions.e: In high-performing teams, members hold each other accountable.

questions.q: Two senior developers strongly disagree about the system architecture, and the debate is starting to become personal. Explain what the project manager should do to resolve the disagreement while keeping the team collaborative.
questions.m: The PM should bring the disagreement into an open, structured discussion that focuses on the technical problem, not on the people, and remind the team of its conflict norms. Each developer presents their option, and the team weighs the pros and cons of both against the project's objectives and data. The PM uses a collaborating (confronting/problem-solving) approach to combine the best parts and works toward consensus, persuading rather than dictating. This produces a durable decision the team commits to (buy-in and clarity) and keeps trust intact instead of pushing the conflict underground.

questions.q: When is a predictive approach more appropriate than an adaptive approach? Give a situation for each.
questions.m: A predictive approach fits when the project and product requirements can be defined, collected and analysed at the start and stay stable, or when there is a big investment and high risk that need frequent reviews and change control, for example a payroll system built to fixed legal rules. An adaptive approach fits when requirements are uncertain and volatile and will be refined from user feedback in short iterations, for example a startup's new social app. Predictive reduces uncertainty early with upfront planning; adaptive manages it by learning as it goes.

questions.q: Explain the difference between contingency reserve and management reserve, including who controls each.
questions.m: Contingency reserve is money or time set aside for identified risks so the planned response can be paid for if they happen; it is part of the cost baseline and controlled by the project manager. Management reserve is set aside for unknown events and unplanned in-scope work; it sits on top of the cost baseline in the total budget and is usually controlled by upper management, the sponsor, or the PMO.

questions.q: Explain how organizational culture can affect project planning, and give an example.
questions.m: Activity estimation is imprecise, so the culture decides how honest people are when they estimate. Where lateness is punished, team members give wider (padded) estimates to protect themselves, which makes plans unrealistic. In a culture of trust, people give honest assessments. For example, developers who are publicly criticized for missing dates start doubling every estimate, while a team that discusses misses openly gives realistic ones.

questions.q: A software company has only two security specialists but runs six projects that need them. Explain why a matrix structure fits this company, and describe one problem it creates for the specialists.
questions.m: A matrix creates a dual hierarchy in which functional departments and projects have equal prominence. It fits this company because it maximizes scarce resources: the two specialists stay in their functional security group and are loaned to all six projects as needed, instead of each project hiring its own. The problem is that each specialist has two bosses, the functional manager and the project managers, so they get caught between competing demands, and managers have to negotiate to share their time.

questions.q: Explain the difference between technical leadership and adaptive leadership, and when a project manager should use each.
questions.m: Technical leadership is used when a problem can be solved by known means: the leader directs, instructs and applies best practice, motivating through their vision and personality (expertise, confidence). Adaptive leadership is used when the problem cannot be solved by known means: the leader facilitates learning, leads with good questions and keeps the team anchored to a shared sense of purpose, motivating through visible progress. Most IT projects mix both, so an adaptive leader can delegate the known problems to someone who leads technically.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a model, a method, and an artifact, with an example of each.
questions.m: A model is a thinking strategy that explains a process, framework or phenomenon, e.g. the Tuckman ladder for team development. A method is the means for achieving an outcome, output or deliverable, e.g. estimating or a daily stand-up. An artifact is a template, document, output or deliverable, e.g. a risk register or project charter.

questions.q: Explain why a project team would tailor its approach and describe two benefits of tailoring.
questions.m: Tailoring is the deliberate adaptation of the project management approach, governance and processes so they suit the environment and the work. Teams tailor because each project is different: a critical nuclear-reactor project needs far more rigor than an office building, and teams must balance competing demands such as speed, cost, quality and compliance. Benefits include more commitment from team members who helped tailor the approach, a customer-oriented focus, and more efficient use of project resources.
